extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and graduate students in communication/media studies
extracted.subtask_short: building a theory of news content
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter excerpt laying out hypotheses and research guidance (the hierarchy of influences model) for how ideological, organizational, routine, and individual-level forces shape news content and newsworthiness. It proposes testable propositions about inclusion, stereotyping, foreign coverage, elite influence, and recommended multi-level research approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance increases news inclusion and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: The more deviant people or events are, the more likely they are to be included in media content and the more likely they are to be stereotyped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The media help maintain the boundaries of social order by showing what is approved and not approved. Deviant people and events may be trivialized or shown as dangerous. This is apparently true of the U.S. media, regardless of whether they are covering people or events in the United States or in another country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/economic/cultural significance predicts foreign coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more political, economic, or cultural significance one country has for another, the more the former will appear in the latter's mass media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such social system-level attachments between countries affect priorities in media coverage. Although the same news values may apply for domestic and foreign news coverage, measures of political, economic, and cultural significance affect what is considered important, one of the main criteria for establishing newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective routines withheld outside legitimate controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists will not use objective routines, such as balance, when subjects are outside the area of legitimate controversy and in the areas of consensus or deviance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies that 'objectivity' or balancing practices are applied selectively—primarily within contested arenas—rather than uniformly across all subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elites act collectively when ideological principles threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: Elites will respond to media as a class when core ideological principles are threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions of business, for example, will be more unified and coordinated, transcending the actions of any given company or industry, as more capitalist values come under attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite connections increase ideological consistency in media
rubrics_metrics.description: The more closely media are connected to other elites, the more media content will be consistent with those elite ideological viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of elite connections include board interlocks and club memberships; such ties make media content more aligned with elite perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair of violations to preserve occupational paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of occupational paradigms—anomalies—must be repaired in order to preserve the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This repair is most evident when the violation crosses important ideological boundaries; institutions and practitioners will take steps to reestablish accepted norms and frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television is more ideologically charged than print
rubrics_metrics.description: On a given issue, television coverage will be more ideologically charged than the print media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a comparative hypothesis about medium effects on ideological tone of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple levels of analysis (hierarchy of influences model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaching media studies from several levels (individual, routines, organizational, social system, ideological) yields a fuller understanding than any single perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any single perspective does not present a complete picture; many studies observe at one level and then make inferences about higher levels—e.g., individual bias does not automatically translate into media bias. The model encourages awareness of multiple perspectives to keep thinking open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop interlevel links between routines, organizations, and ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple levels of analysis to examine connections: occupational routines relate to larger ideological requirements; personal values of journalists cannot be separated from their routines; organizational structure is related to media routines; ideological forces must work through people and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying how ideological forces operate through routines and practices is an important direction for future research—development of interlevel links is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity between lower-level studies and higher-level theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies at lower levels of analysis should be informed by theories of power and society developed at higher levels, and ideological-level studies should be conditioned by an understanding of individuals and their practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizing theory and research this way is recommended to achieve greater theoretical and methodological precision; combining insights across levels produces a more complete understanding of the mass media's role in society.
